name: American Arts and Crafts

description.short: Craftsman, bungalow, and Prairie — the American translation of the British reform argument into a mass-market house that millions actually bought.
description.long:
Britain produced the philosophy and a few hundred houses for wealthy clients. America produced hundreds of thousands of houses and shipped them by catalog. Gustav Stickley's *The Craftsman* magazine ran from 1901 to 1916 and distributed plans directly to readers; Sears, Aladdin, and dozens of plan services did the rest.

The result is the only moment in American history when a reform movement grounded in material honesty and craft became the default choice of ordinary buyers. It ended for economic reasons — the bungalow's exposed structure and heavy timber were expensive, and the Depression killed it — not because anyone argued it down.

defining_characteristics: Structure expressed rather than concealed: rafter tails, brackets, beams, joinery
Low horizontal massing with very deep eave overhangs
The porch under the primary roof as an outdoor room
Open planning around a hearth, replacing the formal parlor
Mass distribution by magazine and mail-order catalog
